concepts.def: The mass of product that would form if every reactant particle reacted exactly as the balanced equation shows and none of the product was lost. It is the largest mass that could possibly be made, so it is the figure the mass actually obtained is compared with.

concepts.term: Conservation of mass in a reaction
concepts.def: No atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction. A shortfall on the balance therefore never means that atoms have disappeared; it means atoms are somewhere other than in the product that was collected and weighed.

A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants. Such a reaction does not go to completion, so some reactant is always still present and the amount of product obtained is below the theoretical maximum.

Product left behind when it is separated from the reaction mixture, for example crystals clinging to the filter paper or the beaker, or solid still dissolved in the liquid poured away. It was made but never weighed, so the yield falls.

A reaction in which some of the reactants react in ways different to the expected reaction, forming a substance other than the desired product. The atoms are all still present but they are locked into the wrong compound.
The amount of a product obtained from a reaction. It is a measured quantity, found by weighing the product after it has been separated from the mixture, washed and dried.
The amount of product obtained compared with the maximum theoretical amount, expressed as a percentage: % Yield = (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) x 100.

concepts.term: Finding a theoretical mass from the balanced equation
concepts.def: Convert the given mass of reactant to moles, use the balancing numbers in the equation to find the moles of the desired product, then multiply by the relative formula mass of that product. The balancing numbers must be used or the answer is out by that factor.

A measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products. It is worked out from the balanced equation alone, using relative formula masses, so it is fixed for a given reaction whatever happens in the laboratory.

concepts.term: Why a high atom economy matters
concepts.def: A reaction with a high atom economy turns more of the starting materials into the product that is wanted. This is important for sustainable development, because raw materials are limited and waste has to be dealt with, and for economic reasons, because unused starting material and waste disposal both cost money.

(Relative formula mass of desired product from equation) / (Sum of relative formula masses of all reactants from equation) x 100. Every reactant in the equation counts in the bottom line, each multiplied by its balancing number.

mcqs.q: No atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction, yet the mass of product collected is almost always less than the calculated amount. What does this shortfall show?
options: A few of the atoms are destroyed as the old bonds are broken apart.
Mass is conserved only when a reaction is done in a sealed flask.
The atoms all still exist, but they are not all in the product.
The balanced equation overstates how much product could form.
mcqs.explain: Correct: no atoms are gained or lost, so the missing mass is unreacted material, product lost on separation, or atoms built into a different product.

mcqs.q: A product is made using a reaction that is reversible. Why does this keep the yield below the maximum theoretical amount?
options: The reaction does not go to completion, so some reactant is left over.
All of the product turns back into the reactants, and none is left.
Atoms are used up by the backward reaction and cannot be got back.
The backward reaction uses up the catalyst, so the reaction ends.
mcqs.explain: Correct: product re-forms reactant as fast as reactant forms product, so the mixture always still contains some reactant.

mcqs.q: Copper sulfate crystals are filtered from the reaction mixture, washed and dried before being weighed. Which reason for a low yield does this practical show?
options: Filtering strips atoms out of the compound, so it now weighs less.
Water driven off during drying shows mass is not conserved.
Washing adds impurities to the crystals and lowers the mass.
Some product stays on the filter paper and inside the glassware.
mcqs.explain: Correct: product lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture is never weighed, so the yield falls below the maximum.

mcqs.q: A student analyses the product mixture and finds an unexpected second compound in it. Which reason for the reduced yield does this point to?
options: The reaction is reversible, so some product has changed back again.
Some reactant reacted in a way different to the expected one.
Filtering and washing took some atoms out of the product itself.
The relative formula masses used in the calculation were wrong.
mcqs.explain: Correct: a compound that does not appear in the equation shows that some of the reactants took a different reaction pathway.

mcqs.q: What does the percentage yield of a reaction tell you?
options: The percentage of the product that has not turned back into reactants.
The mass of product made, as a percentage of the maximum theoretical mass.
The mass of product made, as a percentage of the mass of the reactants.
The percentage of reactant atoms ending up in the useful product.
mcqs.explain: Correct: the amount of product obtained is the yield, and comparing it with the maximum theoretical amount as a percentage gives the percentage yield.

mcqs.q: Which calculation gives the percentage yield of a product?
options: (maximum theoretical mass of product / mass of the product made) x 100
(mass of product actually made / total mass of all reactants) x 100
(Mr of the desired product / sum of Mr of all reactants) x 100
(mass of product actually made / maximum theoretical mass) x 100
mcqs.explain: Correct: the specification formula is % Yield = (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) x 100.

mcqs.q: 6.0 g of magnesium is burned in air. The maximum theoretical mass of magnesium oxide is 10.0 g. The student collects 8.5 g of magnesium oxide. What is the percentage yield?
The maximum theoretical mass of a product is 60 g. A student separates and dries the product and obtains 54 g of it. What is the percentage yield?
Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Mr: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56, CO2 = 44. What is the maximum theoretical mass of calcium oxide that can be made from 10 g of calcium carbonate?
options: 4 g
mcqs.explain: Correct: 10 / 100 = 0.1 mol of CaCO3, which gives 0.1 mol of CaO, so the mass is 0.1 x 56 = 5.6 g.

mcqs.q: Iron is extracted in the blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Mr: Fe2O3 = 160, Fe = 56. What is the maximum theoretical mass of iron that can be made from 20 g of iron(III) oxide?
options: 7 g
mcqs.explain: Correct: 20 / 160 = 0.125 mol of Fe2O3, and the 2 in 2Fe gives 0.25 mol of Fe, so the mass is 0.25 x 56 = 14 g.

mcqs.q: What does the atom economy of a reaction measure?
options: The amount of the starting materials that ends up as useful product.
The amount of the predicted product that is collected in practice.
The amount of reactant that has reacted once equilibrium has been set up.
The amount of the energy given out that is transferred usefully.
mcqs.explain: Correct: atom economy, or atom utilisation, is a measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products.

mcqs.q: A student weighs out the reactants, weighs the product she has made and divides one measured mass by the other to find the atom economy. Why is this wrong?
options: The mass lost when the product was separated must be subtracted.
The atom economy changes when the reaction is scaled up to industry.
The percentage atom economy is calculated using the balanced equation.
The actual yield of product is needed as well as the theoretical.
mcqs.explain: Correct: the specification calculates atom economy from relative formula masses in the balanced equation, so measured masses are never used.

mcqs.q: In the percentage atom economy calculation, what is the bottom line of the fraction?
options: The relative formula mass of the desired product from the equation.
The sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants in the equation.
The relative formula mass of the one reactant that the product comes from.
The total mass of all the reactants weighed out in the experiment.
mcqs.explain: Correct: the Mr of the desired product is divided by the sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants from the equation.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen is made from methane: CH4 + H2O -> 3H2 + CO. Mr: CH4 = 16, H2O = 18, H2 = 2, CO = 28. What is the percentage atom economy for making hydrogen?
Titanium is extracted by the reaction TiCl4 + 4Na -> Ti + 4NaCl. Mr: TiCl4 = 190, Na = 23, Ti = 48, NaCl = 58.5. What is the percentage atom economy for titanium?

Two routes make the same product. Route 1: atom economy 42 %, percentage yield 95 %, fast, by-product is waste that must be disposed of. Route 2: atom economy 88 %, percentage yield 90 %, slightly slower, by-product is sold as a fertiliser. Which judgement is best supported by the data?
options: Route 1, because its higher percentage yield means that less is wasted.
Route 1, because a faster rate always makes the process a cheaper one.
Route 2, because a high atom economy always gives a high percentage yield.
Route 2, because much more of the reactant mass ends up as product.
mcqs.explain: Correct: 88 % atom economy with a 90 % yield and a saleable by-product wastes far less raw material, for the cost of a slightly slower rate.

mcqs.q: Give one reason why it is important for a company to use a reaction with a high atom economy.
options: More of the product predicted by the equation is collected each time.
Less of the starting material is wasted, so raw materials cost less.
The reaction runs faster, so more product is made in the same time.
No by-products are made at all, so there is no waste to deal with.
mcqs.explain: Correct: more of the starting material ends up as useful product, which matters for sustainable development, because raw materials are limited, and for economic reasons.
